item.title: Amsterdam university bans laptops and mobiles from lecture hall
item.description:
Amsterdam university bans laptops and mobiles from lecture hall

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Students who have enrolled for a sociology course at the University of Amsterdam this year have been told to leave electronic devices at the door and go back to taking notes by hand.

The UvA has banned laptops, mobile phones and tablets from lectures and classes in interdisciplinary social science, on the grounds that they interefere with students’ concentration.

Senior lecturer Cyrilien Evertsen told NOS that “60% to 80% of students are doing things on digital devices during classes other than listening”, such as shopping or chatting on social media. “They’re not mentally present in the class,” she said.

Paul Kirschner, emeritus professor of educational psychology at Utrecht University, backed the stance, arguing that switching off devices and taking notes by hand makes students engage directly with the lecture material.

“Switch off all electronic devices because it’s a weapon of mass distraction,” he said.

“If you’re checking your email, you’re not following the class,” he said. “You might think that’s not so bad, but research has shown that people to your left and right get distracted and do significantly worse as a result.”

He added that handwriting forced students to select and summarise what information they take down because it is a slower process than typing.

“So you’re digesting the information, and learning is digesting,” he said.

item.title: Amsterdam man arrested over links to ShinyHunters hacking group
item.description:
Amsterdam man arrested over links to ShinyHunters hacking group

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A 24-year-old man from Amsterdam has been arrested on suspicion of involvement with the hacking group ShinyHunters, which has been behind a number of large-scale attacks on Dutch businesses in the past year.

Police said on social media that he was arrested this month and will appear in court in Rotterdam on Wednesday.

Sources told broadcaster NOS that the suspect is Pepijn van der S., who was sentenced to four years in prison in 2023 for extortion, money laundering and hacking. He was released this year.

Van der S. reportedly has a background in legitimate cybersecurity, having worked for Amsterdam-based security firm Hadrian. He also carried out ethical hacking research with the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure. At the same time, he was leaking data stolen from clients and other companies, the court found in 2023.

ShinyHunters was responsible for an attack on Dutch telecoms provider Odido earlier this year, in which millions of customers had their personal data stolen. After the company refused to pay a ransom, the group posted much of the data on the dark web.

The hackers were also behind an attack on Canvas, an online learning platform used by students, after which its parent company paid a ransom to prevent further disruption.

Last week, ShinyHunters also claimed to have accessed the details of thousands of employees at the FBI, the US federal law enforcement agency. The FBI said an investigation was underway.

item.title: Amsterdam wants simpler rules to get asylum seekers working
item.description:
Amsterdam wants simpler rules to get asylum seekers working

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam is making a scheme to help asylum seekers find paid work a permanent fixture, after a pilot involving over 1,000 refugees managed to get 332 of them into jobs in just over 18 months.

The city council is also calling on the national government to make it easier for employers to hire asylum seekers, by scrapping the work permit they currently need.

“It is important that asylum seekers get the chance to work while their application is still being processed,” work and income chief Sofyan Mbarki said in a statement. “Work gives people self-esteem and an income, and it helps them integrate quickly.”

Participants were recruited at three locations: the Willinklaan refugee centre and the emergency shelters at the A&O Hostel in Zuidoost and on board the MS Galaxy, a cruise ship that is being temporarily used to house asylum seekers.

National plans
Mbarki said the results backed up last week’s advice by the socio-economic council, which said councils should be legally required to help newcomers find work that matches their skills.

He also welcomed plans by work and participation minister Thierry Aartsen (VVD) to have councils help 75,000 more people into work, but said councils would need funding from The Hague to do it.

Drop-out risk
The pilot officially ends this year but will continue for another 4 years, as set out in the city’s coalition agreement.

The evaluation, by urban research institute Platform31, found that work gave participants more financial stability and helped their language skills. Employers described them as motivated and keen to learn.

It also recommended more aftercare and job coaching in the first months, to reduce the number of people who drop out of jobs after being placed.

Amsterdam wants the work permit (tewerkstellingsvergunning) replaced with a simple obligation to notify the UWV, the system already used for displaced Ukrainians in the Netherlands.

item.title: Apartment block evacuated after fire breaks out in Apeldoorn
item.description:
Apartment block evacuated after fire breaks out in Apeldoorn

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dozens of people had to be evacuated from a block of flats in Apeldoorn after a fire broke out in the early hours of Tuesday.

Residents of 30 apartments were told to leave their homes after firefighters were called out to the complex on Wagenstraat at around 2am, where a third-floor flat was ablaze.

Two people were taken to hospital as a precaution after inhaling smoke, local newspaper De Stentor reported. Five others were checked over by paramedics at the scene.

Firefighters used a cherry-picker to reach people who were unable to leave their apartments via the fire escape.

Police believe the fire may have been started deliberately. Enquiries are ongoing.

item.title: More people dying from falls, 21 a day on average: CBS
item.description:
More people dying from falls, 21 a day on average: CBS

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of people who died after an accidental fall in the Netherlands rose again last year, to 7,810 – an average of 21 per day – according to new figures from national statistics office CBS.

The figure is 480 more than in 2024, and falls are the most common non-natural cause of death in the Netherlands, CBS said.

The numbers cover people who trip, slip or fall and die within 30 days. Falls involving a vehicle, such as a bike or mobility scooter, are counted as traffic accidents and are not included.

Most victims are elderly: 79% were 80 or older and just 2% were under 60. Women accounted for 60% of deaths among people in their eighties and 72% among the over-90s.

The rise is not only down to the ageing population. Even when adjusted for age and population growth, the death rate from falls has gone up every year for the past 15 years. The CBS reported a similar increase two years ago.

The sharpest rise is among women aged 90 and over. In 2025, 2.1% of all women in that age group died after a fall, compared with 1% in 2016.

More fatal falls happen in winter than in summer – over the past five years, 28% of fatal falls among men and 27% among women took place in winter, compared with 22% and 23% in summer.

Of the 7,330 people who died after a fall in 2024, some 5,000 were receiving long-term care, most of them living in care institutions. Falls caused 7.7% of all deaths in care institutions that year.

The figures were published to coincide with fall prevention week, run by the health ministry and safety organisation VeiligheidNL.

item.title: Growing number of Dutch believe hitting wives acceptable: study
item.description:
Growing number of Dutch believe hitting wives acceptable: study

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More people in the Netherlands believe hitting a wife can be acceptable, according to a long-running survey of Dutch values by the University of Amsterdam and Tilburg University.

Just over 84% of those questioned this year said wife beating could never be justified, down from 87% in 2022 and 88% in 2012, news agency ANP reported on Tuesday. The figures come from the Dutch part of the World Values Survey, an international study of public opinion, which questioned 2,500 adults.

“The trend is still the same,” UvA researcher Mark Boukes told ANP. “The number of people who think it is never justifiable to hit their wife – in other words, resistance to hitting a woman – is falling.”

Young people were less likely than older people to reject domestic violence outright. The researchers also found that people who feel financially secure tend to hold more progressive views.

Women feel less safe
Women said they feel less safe than in earlier surveys and are particularly worried about sexual harassment. The researchers cite the murder of 17-year-old Lisa in 2025 as a possible reason for the change.

The study also pointed to the influence of the manosphere, the online movement promoting hostility towards women. “A lot is changing in society that is leading people to hold more conservative opinions,” Boukes said.

Judith Tielen, the junior education minister responsible for gender equality policy, called the findings “alarming”. “It shows we really still have a lot to do to eliminate violence against women,” the right-wing liberal VVD politician told ANP.

Tielen has also commissioned research into the spread of anti-gender narratives and their links to the manosphere and other extremist movements. The cabinet appointed its first national coordinator on violence against women in July.

Round-the-clock chat
The survey findings came as Veilig Thuis, the national advice and reporting centre for domestic violence and child abuse, said its online chat service is now available 24/7. Its phone line already ran around the clock, but the chat was only staffed during office hours.

The extended hours were introduced quietly a month ago. In August, three times as many people sought advice through the chat as a year earlier, and there are now more chats outside office hours than during them, broadcaster NOS reported.

“We see a peak when people get home from work, and another before bedtime, around 11pm,” Elijah Sanches, a doctor who staffs the chat, told NOS. “I talk to people who hear noise at their neighbours’, or women chatting from the toilet because their partner is shouting at them and hitting them.”

Veilig Thuis received 136,000 reports last year. It is legally required to assess the risk in each case within five days, but in recent years it has taken longer in almost half of cases, and the health inspectorate has repeatedly said this must improve.

The chat is intended for advice, not formal reports, and Veilig Thuis hopes it will help filter out cases that do not need investigation. “Some people who make a report now really only need advice,” Sanches said. “That saves time, so we can investigate the reports that come in more quickly.”

If you have experienced or are experiencing domestic or sexual violence, Veilig Thuis (Safe at Home) offers confidential advice 24 hours a day on 0800 2000 or at veiligthuis.nl. In an emergency, call 112.

item.title: Jetten apologises for call to punch abusers “hard in the face”
item.description:
Jetten apologises for call to punch abusers “hard in the face”

September 29, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prime minister Rob Jetten has apologised for saying people who attack women and minorities deserved to be “punched in the face” during a party conference appearance at the weekend.

Jetten said he regretted his “spontaneous reaction” to a question from the conference floor about attacks on women, gays and minorities.

“We won’t let those guys win. We’re going to punch them hard in the face,” he replied, accompanying the last words with a punching gesture.

The question came up during a question and answer session following Jetten’s speech to the 60th anniversary conference of his D66 party.

“I didn’t mean it literally, I’m just really passionate about equal rights and that’s what I tried to convey,” he said in parliament on Tuesday. “I will try to avoid that kind of slip of the tongue in future.”

“Speechless”

Opposition MPs tabled questions about Jetten‘s choice of words. Mona Keijzer, an independent MP who split from the farmers’ party BBB, said she was “speechless”.

Marianne van den Anker, ombudsman in Rotterdam, also criticised Jetten’s choice of words as “unworthy of the prime minister”.

“I think the interviewer should have stepped in,” she told breakfast TV show WNL. “This is promoting violence.”

“We gaan ze vol op hun bek slaan”, zei premier Rob Jetten over mensen die lhbti’ers, vrouwen en minderheden aanvallen. “Premier onwaardig. item.title: Inspectors demand urgent action on youth detention centres
item.description:
Inspectors demand urgent action on youth detention centres

September 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Staff shortages at the Dutch youth detention centres are putting detainees and staff under “persistent and serious” pressure and threatening their safety, three government inspectorates have warned.

Around 450 young people who have been convicted of a crime or are suspected of one are held in the country’s six youth detention centres, known as JJIs. The centres take young people who were aged between 12 and 23 when they committed the offence, though most are between 14 and 21.

Unlike adult prisons, they are meant to focus on education and treatment rather than punishment, to reduce the risk of reoffending.

In a letter to junior justice minister Claudia van Bruggen, the justice, education and health and youth care inspectorates said young people held in the centres are the victims of an “ever-increasing, worrying” erosion of care, treatment, education and daily activities. They called for an urgent action plan.

“Temporary emergency measures such as a shortened daily programme have now become standard practice,” said Elske van Amelsfort, chief inspector at the justice and security inspectorate. “That is why an action plan is needed from the state secretary in the short term.”

By law, young people in JJIs should spend 77 hours a week in group activities. Emergency measures introduced in 2023 set a reduced floor of 62 hours. The inspectorates said the centres are not meeting the requirements of either, because daily programmes are regularly cut back or cancelled at short notice when staff are unavailable.

As a result, young people spend too much time in their rooms, miss school and leave, and cannot always contact their families. Young people told inspectors they found it frustrating to be kept in their rooms, often without warning, and that repeatedly broken promises made it harder to stay motivated.

Warning signs
The inspectorates also said staff are becoming less experienced and more overstretched. Staff are regularly moved at short notice to units where they do not know the young people, which makes it harder to spot warning signs in time. The constant turnover of supervisors is causing frustration and tension among both young people and staff.

The inspectorates have raised concerns about the centres since 2019. The decision to phase out freelance staff in 2025 made the staffing crisis worse, the letter said.

In July, children’s ombudsman Margrite Kalverboer said there had been barely any improvement since the inspectorates’ previous warning a year earlier. She said almost all children’s rights were being violated in the youth detention centres.

item.title: Pro tables bill to remove abortion from Dutch criminal code
item.description:
Pro tables bill to remove abortion from Dutch criminal code

September 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Opposition party Pro has put forward a bill to remove abortion from the Dutch criminal code and officially regulate it as a part of healthcare. Currently, abortion is still technically a crime, although allowed under specific circumstances by professionals.

MP Lisa Vliegenthart, a former midwife, handed the bill to campaigners from feminist group Dolle Mina outside parliament on Monday morning, broadcaster NOS reported.

“This is incredibly important because abortion is healthcare, and as far as I am concerned healthcare has no place in the criminal code,” she said. “That is why we want to remove abortion from the criminal code and include it in healthcare legislation.”

Already legal
Abortion has been legal in the Netherlands since the 1980s, but the legal framework is unusual. Under an article of the criminal code, performing an abortion is a crime. The exception is if it is carried out by a doctor in a licensed clinic or hospital under the conditions set out in the Termination of Pregnancy Act.

Those conditions include a limit of 24 weeks and a requirement that the woman indicates she is in a situation of distress. Women themselves cannot be prosecuted for having abortions, but people administering them can be.

Pro says it wants to keep all the current care requirements, including the time limit, but move them into healthcare law. “Of course abortion has to be carried out carefully,” Vliegenthart said. “But you don’t need the criminal code for that.”
Proponents of the bill say that having abortion in the criminal code adds to the stigma around it and makes the rules harder to update.

The current law was a hard-fought compromise, passed by 76 votes to 74 in the lower house in 1980 and by 38 to 37 in the Senate. The rules have since been loosened, with the mandatory five-day waiting period was scrapped in 2023, and family doctors can now prescribe the abortion pill.

VVD support
Whether the bill passes depends largely on the right-wing liberal VVD. In 2023, the VVD joined the CDA, ChristenUnie, PVV, SGP and FvD to vote down a similar attempt to remove abortion from the criminal code. But its 2025 election manifesto committed the party to “actively work” to do so.

With support from the VVD, D66 and smaller opposition parties, the bill could have a narrow majority. However, the parties’ coalition partner, the CDA, remains against it.

The VVD has not yet said whether it will back the bill. “We are going to read the proposal and wait for the Council of State’s response,” the party said.

Constitution
If the bill passes, Pro wants to go further and enshrine the right to abortion in the Dutch constitution, as France did in 2024. Vliegenthart pointed to the United States, where the Supreme Court overturned the federal right to abortion in 2022. “That pressure exists in Europe and the Netherlands too,” she said.

In practice, access rather than legality is often the bigger issue for women. Last month, the health inspectorate allowed the country’s only online abortion service, which now issues around a quarter of all abortion pills, to keep operating after it changed its practices.

item.title: Market watchdog calls for transparency on AI in price setting
item.description:
Market watchdog calls for transparency on AI in price setting

September 28, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch consumer markets authority ACM has called for more transparency on the role of AI in setting ticket prices after an investigation found wide discrepancies in the amounts charged for airline tickets.

The ACM said some airline seats had 35 different prices, while one-third of tickets cost 40% more than the average price, but there was no easy way for passengers to find the cheapest fare.

ACM chairman Martijn Snoep said the investigation into airline tickets was relevant because “similar techniques are being applied in other sectors”. Online retailers, concert ticket sites and even petrol stations are also using AI to set prices.

Commercial companies are using AI to drive dynamic pricing, based on supply and demand and competitors’ rates, but customers are unable to see how the prices are set.

Sometimes two people looking at the same product at the same time can be charged different prices, the ACM said. The impact of AI also means consumers spend longer searching for the best deal.

“We expect that AI and the availability of data means companies will increasingly use computer-aided prices, including personalised prices,” Snoep said.

The ACM has called on companies to be more open about how they set their prices and explain what factors influence the algorithms.

“Transparency is necessary so we can have a public debate about the desirability and the consequences of this development and how we want to proceed, keeping an eye on the way markets function and preventing people’s vulnerabilities being abused.”
